specPoints.text: understand how the results of experiments involving the dilution of coloured solutions and diffusion of gases can be explained

primer.text: You already know from States of Matter that everything is made of particles, moving differently in solids, liquids and gases. This note turns that model into evidence: two classic experiments, the spread of bromine gas and the fading of a purple solution, only make sense if tiny moving particles really exist. Diffusion and dilution are the particle theory made visible.

lessons.title: Diffusion
lessons.opening: Release bromine gas at the bottom of a jar and, within minutes, the red-brown colour has climbed into a second jar above it. Nothing stirred the gas, yet its particles travelled on their own. That self-driven spreading is called diffusion, and it happens in liquids as well as gases.
keyPoints: Diffusion happens in gases and liquids because their particles are in random motion.
Particles travel from regions of high concentration towards regions where it is low.
Given time, the particles end up evenly spread throughout the available space.
Diffusion needs no energy input, but it speeds up at higher temperatures.
It is slower in liquids than in gases because liquid particles are closely packed and move slowly.

low.restatement: Gas and liquid particles wander randomly, so they drift away from crowded regions into emptier ones until they are spread out evenly.
low.analogy: It is like perfume crossing a quiet room, or a drop of food colouring creeping through still water, with nobody stirring anything.
low.examPointer: Learn the direction of spread, high concentration to low, and that diffusion happens on its own with no energy input.

medium.restatement: Random particle motion carries particles from where they are crowded to where they are scarce, and the spread continues until the concentration is even; heat speeds it up because hotter particles carry more kinetic energy.
medium.analogy: Picture commuters spilling from a packed platform into an empty concourse until everyone stands evenly spaced, and moving faster still when they hurry.
medium.examPointer: The bromine jar experiment is the classic evidence that all matter is made of tiny moving particles, which is what the spec asks you to explain.

check.stem: In which direction do particles diffuse?

options.text: From where they are crowded to where they are scarce
options.explanation: Diffusion carries particles from high concentration to low concentration until the spread is even.

options.text: From low concentration to high concentration
options.explanation: Random motion cannot build a crowd; particles drift away from crowded regions.

options.text: They do not move at all unless heated
options.explanation: Diffusion happens on its own; heating only makes it faster.

options.text: They move only downwards under gravity
options.explanation: Random motion drives the spread, not gravity; bromine climbed into the upper jar.

check.stem: Why does diffusion happen faster at higher temperatures?

options.text: Because the particles have more kinetic energy and move more quickly
options.explanation: Hotter particles carry more kinetic energy, so their random motion spreads them sooner.

options.text: Because the particles become smaller when heated
options.explanation: Particle size never changes with temperature; only the speed of motion does.

options.text: Because heat creates extra particles to spread
options.explanation: Heating adds energy, not particles.

options.text: Because heating widens the gaps between particles permanently
options.explanation: The cause is the faster motion of the particles, not a lasting change in spacing.

check.stem: In the bromine jar demonstration, what allows the air and bromine particles to mix?

options.text: The random motion of both kinds of particle and the large gaps between them
options.explanation: The explanation is random movement combined with the large spaces between gas particles.

options.text: The jars are shaken to stir the gases together
options.explanation: No stirring occurs; the gases mix on their own.

options.text: Bromine particles are lighter, so they float upward
options.explanation: Both gases move randomly in all directions; no floating mechanism is involved.

options.text: A chemical reaction between air and bromine
options.explanation: The gases simply mix physically; no reaction takes place.

check.stem: Why is diffusion slower in liquids than in gases?

options.text: Because liquid particles are closely packed together and move more slowly
options.explanation: Close packing and slower movement make the spread of particles slower in liquids.

options.text: Because liquids contain no moving particles at all
options.explanation: Liquid particles move randomly and slide over each other, so diffusion still occurs.

options.text: Because liquid particles are larger than gas particles
options.explanation: Particle size does not differ between states; packing and speed do.

options.text: Because diffusion is impossible in liquids
options.explanation: Diffusion happens in both gases and liquids, only at different rates.

check.stem: What does the potassium manganate(VII) demonstration show about diffusion in liquids?

options.text: That dissolved particles spread through the water until the colour is even, though slowly
options.explanation: The purple colour spreads through the water over time as particles mix by random motion.

options.text: That the purple colour appears only at the surface of the water
options.explanation: The colour spreads throughout the available space, not just the surface.

options.text: That the crystals dissolve without any particles moving
options.explanation: Dissolving and spreading are themselves particle motion; nothing stays fixed.

options.text: That diffusion in liquids is faster than in gases
options.explanation: The comparison runs the other way: liquids are the slower medium.

lessons.title: Dilution
lessons.opening: Add water to a purple solution and the colour fades step by step, yet it survives many dilutions before it finally disappears. Dilution does not destroy or remove anything: it spreads the same solute particles further apart. How long that faint colour lasts is itself evidence that enormous numbers of very small particles make up even one crystal.
keyPoints: Dilution means adding more solvent, typically water, to an existing solution.
Adding solvent lowers the concentration of the solute particles in the solution.
The solute particles end up more widely separated yet remain in the solution.
The colour grows fainter with each dilution but does not disappear immediately.
The lasting faint colour shows a small crystal must contain a huge number of tiny particles.

low.restatement: Pour in more water and the same coloured particles spread through a bigger volume, so the colour looks fainter with every dilution.
low.analogy: It is like stirring a spoonful of squash into a whole bathtub: the colour is still there, just spread thin through the whole tub.
low.examPointer: Say that dilution spreads particles rather than removing them; the surviving tint is the evidence.

medium.restatement: Each addition of solvent lowers the concentration because the solute particles occupy a larger volume, and the tint survives many dilutions, showing how numerous and small the particles must be.
medium.analogy: Think of the squash again: a whole bathtub still shows a faint tint, so a single spoonful must hold an enormous number of tiny particles.
medium.examPointer: Dilution experiments on coloured solutions, like diffusion experiments on gases, support the kinetic theory of matter.

check.stem: What happens to the solute particles when a solution is diluted?

options.text: They are still present in the solution but more spread out
options.explanation: Dilution spreads the particles through more solvent without removing any of them.

options.text: Some of them are removed along with the extra water
options.explanation: Dilution does not remove particles; it only spreads them out.

options.text: They break apart into smaller particles
options.explanation: The particles remain whole; only their spacing changes.

options.text: They clump together and sink to the bottom
options.explanation: Dilution spreads particles apart; nothing in the process makes them clump.

check.stem: Why does the colour fade only gradually over many dilutions?

options.text: Because even a small crystal contains a very large number of very small particles
options.explanation: The long-lasting colour shows there are a lot of particles in a small amount of the substance.

options.text: Because the water permanently stains the container
options.explanation: The fading happens in the solution itself, not in the container.

options.text: Because new dye particles are created at each step
options.explanation: Dilution creates nothing; the same particles simply spread further.

options.text: Because the particles lose their colour as they spread
options.explanation: The particles keep their properties; the colour looks fainter only because they are more spread out.

check.stem: A student adds water to a coloured solution and expects the colour to vanish at once. What does the experiment actually show?

options.text: The colour becomes fainter with each dilution and persists through many of them
options.explanation: The colour fades but does not disappear until a lot of dilutions have been done.

options.text: The colour disappears completely after a single dilution
options.explanation: That is exactly what the experiment contradicts.

options.text: The colour becomes darker as more water is added
options.explanation: Adding solvent lowers the concentration, so the colour lightens.

options.text: The colour changes from purple to blue
options.explanation: The note describes gradual fading, not a change of hue.

check.stem: What do diffusion and dilution experiments together provide evidence for?

options.text: The kinetic theory of matter: all matter is made of tiny, moving particles
options.explanation: The exam hint names diffusion and dilution as evidence for the kinetic theory of matter.

options.text: That particles exist only in coloured solutions
options.explanation: The evidence covers solids, liquids and gases, as the opening of the note states.

options.text: That energy must always be added for particles to move
options.explanation: Diffusion happens on its own, with no energy input required.

options.text: That particles are at their largest in gases
options.explanation: Neither experiment fixes particle size by state; both depend on motion and spacing.

check.stem: Which addition of water would make the purple colour faintest after a single dilution?

options.text: The largest volume of water, spreading the particles the most
options.explanation: More solvent means a lower concentration, so the biggest dilution gives the faintest colour.

options.text: The smallest volume of water
options.explanation: A small addition changes the concentration the least.

options.text: No water at all, as standing still dilutes best
options.explanation: Dilution specifically means adding solvent; standing changes nothing about the concentration.

options.text: Warming the solution instead of adding water
options.explanation: Warming speeds diffusion, but dilution means adding solvent to lower the concentration.

glossary.definition: The spreading of particles from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration.
How crowded particles are within a given volume of gas or liquid.
The energy of motion; hotter particles carry more of it, so diffusion speeds up.
The process of adding more solvent to a solution, which lowers the concentration.
The liquid, usually water, that is added to dilute a solution.
The dissolved substance whose particles are spread further apart during dilution.
The mixture formed when a solute is dissolved in a solvent.

workedExample.prompt: Bromine vapour is released at the bottom of a sealed jar of air. In a second experiment, purple potassium manganate(VII) solution is diluted with more water. a) Name the process that spreads the bromine and state the direction the particles move. b) Explain why the bromine spreads through the whole jar with no stirring. c) State what happens to the colour as water is added, and what this kind of experiment is evidence for.
steps: a) The bromine spreads by diffusion: its particles move from the region of high concentration at the bottom towards the low-concentration region above.
b) Gas particles are in continuous random motion, so bromine and air particles mix on their own until the bromine is evenly spread through the available space; no energy input is required.
c) Adding water lowers the concentration of the purple particles, so the colour grows fainter with each dilution but does not vanish at once.
Diffusion and dilution experiments like these are evidence for the kinetic theory of matter — enormous numbers of very tiny, constantly moving particles.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Diffusion, from high to low concentration. b) Random particle motion spreads the gas evenly with no energy input. c) The colour fades gradually over repeated dilutions; such experiments evidence the kinetic theory of matter.
